transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2025-02-14 10:00 PST; Duration approx 52 min; Recorded via Fireflies.
Attendees (recorded): Sofia Park (Redwood AE), Michael Chen (Redwood SE), Tina Kapoor (Nimbus CTO), Raj Patel (Lead ML Eng), Priya Iyer (PM).

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, key generation params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop sequences), retry behavior and idempotency, and how Redwood's Console + Optimize help tune throughput/cost. Customer interested in latency guarantees and data retention controls; wants a short POC to validate 95th pct latency under their traffic.

Topics (auto): hosted API demo; streaming chunks and partial outputs; request params and defaults; retry/backoff strategies; idempotency keys; observability in Redwood Console; Optimize recommendations for batching/caching.

00:00 Sofia (AE): All right, good morning everyone, thanks for joining on Valentine's day, appreciate it. I'm Sofia from Redwood, AE — I'll run the first part and Michael will jump into the deep technical demo.
00:14 Tina (CTO): Hi, thanks. Excited to see the hosted flow. We've got about 2 pm folks heads-down, so trying to keep to about 45 min but room for questions.
00:24 Sofia: Yep, totally. Quick agenda: hosted API basics, live demo of chat generation and streaming, latency/cost tradeoffs, then Michael will cover retries and console observability and then we do Q&A. Sound good?
00:31 Priya (PM): Sounds good. We're mostly evaluating for chat assistants in our analytics UI — short prompts usually, sometimes longer followups.
00:45 Sofia: Great. Raj, you had noted current stack is GKE + a small in-house sharded service for prompt routing — is that correct?
00:53 Raj (Eng): Yeah we run on GKE, mostly nodejs microservices. We currently call OpenAI endpoints directly. We do some client-side retry logic.
01:05 Michael (SE): Hey all. I'll jump in on the demo piece — I'll show the hosted API chat endpoint, streaming mode, show how partial tokens appear in the client, then simulate a transient failure to show retry patterns.
01:20 Sofia: Quick qualification — any strict requirements on data residency or retention? Are you allowed to use hosted endpoints or do you need private/VPC?
01:31 Tina: For now hosted is fine for non-PII, but any logs touching customer identifiers must be retained for 30 days and then purged. SOC 2 is a plus.
01:45 Sofia: Noted. We have SOC 2 + ISO docs, and hosted offers token-level retention controls + option for Private deployment later. We'll send the security whitepaper after the call.
01:56 Raj: Also curious on latency SLOs — we need consistent 95th pct under 400ms for short prompts. Is that realistic on hosted?
02:08 Michael: So for short prompts (<=128 tokens) on our curated small-medium models we regularly hit sub-200ms p50 and 95th is typically around 350-450ms depending on concurrency and batching config. We'll show latency numbers in the Console.
02:27 Sofia: Ok demo time — Michael, take it away.
02:31 Michael: Cool. I'm sharing my screen. Starting with a simple POST to /v1/chat/completions — in streaming mode you add ?stream=true or set the "stream" param depending on SDK. The response is a series of events, each with partial tokens.
02:49 [screen click sounds]
02:52 Michael: Example here — prompt: "You are an analytics assistant. Summarize last session in three bullets." you'll see the client receives chunks: "Summary:", then "- High-level...". Streaming is low-latency because we flush tokens as they're ready.
03:14 Priya: Do you send token-level events over HTTP SSE or do you use websockets?
03:20 Michael: We support chunked HTTP streaming (SSE-like) out of the box for our hosted API and native SDKs have helpers to reassemble. Websocket support is available for higher concurrency use cases.
03:34 Raj: How are partial tokens handled on retries? If we retry do we get duplicates in the UI?
03:40 Michael: Good question. There are two pieces: first, idempotency at request level — you can provide an idempotency_key to prevent duplicate completions. Second, streaming retries are usually handled client-side by aborting the stream and retrying the full request; we recommend using idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations or dedup logic on client when partial tokens are already rendered.
04:05 Sofia: To add, if you use our SDKs we expose a high-level stream API that supports resume points in some cases — but network disconnects often mean you re-request and dedupe on message-id or idempotency.
04:20 Priya: Hmm ok. We'd prefer not to show duplicate lines to end-users.
04:25 Michael: Understood. We'll share the sample code patterns.

05:00 Michael: Next: params. Typical fields — temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop sequences, presence_penalty. For chat we also pass conversation history as messages with roles.
05:20 Michael: Temperature controls randomness; for deterministic system messages we set temperature 0. For creative summaries we might 0.7. top_p can be used instead or in tandem.
05:36 Raj: What about token limits and costs? Are streaming responses cheaper?
05:42 Sofia: Cost is per-token generated + per-token input, streaming vs non-streaming doesn't change the token count — it's an API behavior, not billing. So chunking doesn't save cost but helps latency and perceived speed.
05:58 Raj: Right. Ok.

06:30 Michael: I'm going to show a quick live run with a short prompt to demo streaming. [typing] Starting request... you can see first token at 6:36, then subsequent chunks at 6:36-6:42 range.
06:40 [client audio: small keyboard clacks]
06:42 Michael: Chunk 1: "Summary:" chunk 2: "- The session showed a bump in..." -- chunks keep streaming.
07:05 Tina: Looks good — any guarantees on chunk size or flush frequency?
07:12 Michael: It's heuristic — the runtime flushes when token buffers reach a threshold or at sentence boundaries; not a strict per-token flush. We can tune engine behavior per model config for certain workloads.
07:28 Priya: On the Console, can we visualize streaming latencies?
07:33 Michael: We show request-level latency (connect, first-byte, and total), and in the logs you can see time-to-first-chunk. That helps diagnose perceived latency.
07:50 Sofia: Quick pause: anyone running server-side batching on your side?
07:55 Raj: Currently no, we do per-request forwarded to OpenAI with simple concurrency limiter.
08:04 Sofia: Ok, good. If you want to optimize cost with Redwood Optimize we recommend workload profiling first — then batching + prefix caching suggestions. For chat, prefix/KV cache helps a lot if you have repeated system prompts or repeated context.
08:22 Raj: Interesting. Could you give an example impact?
08:25 Michael: Sure — in a demo tenant we reduced tokens by 18-28% just by caching common system messages and rerouting repeated context into cached embeddings for re-use. We'll include a Optimize report sample.

09:00 Michael: Now simulate a transient failure — I'm going to drop the network on my client to simulate socket close. [clicks] On the server we see a connection reset; client code will observe a terminated stream.
09:18 Michael: If you retry immediately without idempotency, the model could generate a different completion — that's expected. If you need exactly-once semantics, use idempotency_key or design the flow to be reentrant.
09:30 Priya: So idempotency key prevents double billing?
09:34 Michael: Idempotency_key ensures we won't process duplicate requests server-side; billing is tied to processing, so if the first attempt hit the model fully, retry won't be billed again if the key matches and the original completed. If the first never completed, the retry will process and bill as normal.
09:50 Tina: Good. For our legal folks we need a writeup on idempotency and billing semantics.
09:58 Sofia: We'll include that in the security packet.

10:20 Raj: On retries/backoff: recommended strategy? Exponential backoff with jitter?
10:26 Michael: Yes. Exponential backoff with capped retries (3-5), and for streaming we suggest larger initial backoff so you don't retry during model tail-generation. Use status codes: 429 -> backoff, 500/502/503 similar; for connection aborts you may retry once quickly then backoff.
10:46 Raj: And rate limiting? We hit bursts during analytics runs.
10:49 Sofia: Hosted has rate limits per API key / plan, but we can map to token-level quotas or burst allowances. For Dedicated you get reserved GPU capacity and different SLAs.
11:03 Priya: If we start hosted and then want to move to Dedicated later, how seamless is that?
11:09 Michael: We support pinning model versions and identical API surface; moving to Dedicated involves provisioning capacity, but the SDK calls/params remain the same. You may need to adjust autoscaling and batching configs.
11:22 Tina: Security again: do you do KMS integration for model keys?
11:28 Sofia: For Private deployments yes; for hosted we manage keys but we support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own KMS) for enterprise. We also offer log redaction and token-level retention policies.

12:00 [brief pause while Michael flips tab]
12:08 Michael: Now I'll show Console — per-route analytics: tokens, cost, latency histograms, and a streaming trace view. This shows a failed request and retry timeline, so you can correlate increases in 95th pct to retries or hot-spots.
12:35 Raj: Nice, that should help root-cause. Can we instrument user-id tagging in logs?
12:39 Michael: Yes you can pass metadata fields (like user_id) on requests that are stored in traces and logs — we encrypt at rest and PII can be redacted via rules.
12:52 Priya: For the POC, we want a test harness that simulates 50 rps with our prompt mix — can Redwood accept that load on hosted?
13:05 Sofia: Possibly; it depends on model size and concurrency. For early POC we often recommend a small reserved burst or Dedicated trial to ensure stability. We can estimate cost with your 50 rps profile.
13:20 Raj: We'll send traffic numbers.

14:00 Tina: One concern: streaming UX on mobile — do you support partial rendering with update diffs? We have clients updating DOM and worry about flicker.
14:12 Michael: Our SDKs include helpers to provide incremental deltas and token-level patching to reduce flicker. We'll share the mobile helper code.

14:30 Priya: Questions about function calling? We also want structured outputs from models sometimes.
14:36 Michael: Hosted API supports function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs. In streaming mode you get the function call fields as they are produced; sometimes you'll see the JSON build up chunk-by-chunk — we recommend validating final parse on complete response.

15:00 [interruption, someone mutes/unmutes]
15:10 Raj: Any gotchas around streaming + function calls?
15:14 Michael: If you rely on partial JSON for early client actions, be careful — incomplete JSON will fail parsing. Use our SDK that buffers until a valid parse or use separate event messages for function call intents.

16:00 Tina: We're interested in cost controls — throttles, quotas, and per-route budgets.
16:08 Sofia: Console supports per-route quotas and alerting; we can also set token budgets and send alerts at thresholds. For enterprise customers we can integrate billing alerts into your finance SLAs.

17:00 Priya: Time check— we're at about 17 minutes into the demo, can we see a quick end-to-end flow for a chat with retries?
17:10 Michael: Sure — I'm going to re-run a prompt, simulate a 503 halfway, show logs that indicate connection reset at ~17:25, and then client retries with idempotency key causing service to return the cached response.
17:30 [demo run audible] 
17:46 Michael: In the Console trace you can see initial request id abc123, handshake then chunked tokens for 3s, connection abort, then retry with same idempotency key returns cached response.
18:02 Raj: That solves the duplicate UX issue for us.
18:08 Tina: Good. Could we get sample code for Node and iOS?
18:12 Michael: Yep, we'll attach both.

19:00 Priya: On Optimize — you mentioned cached system prompts and quantization suggestions. Can you summarize how that flow works?
19:08 Michael: Optimize runs a profiling job on a sample of your traffic; it outputs recommendations: batch size targets, whether to enable prefix/KV cache for certain conversation patterns, and if a smaller quantized model will meet your latency-quality tradeoff. It's advisory but with expected cost savings estimates.
19:30 Priya: How invasive is quantization? Any quality regressions?
19:35 Michael: Depends on model and evals. We do AB evals on your prompt set; some workloads see negligible regression for 8-bit quantization, others may want 4-bit with more testing. We'll recommend model variants and show eval diffs.

20:30 Tina: Ok, next steps recap?
20:33 Sofia: I'll recap then we'll open for final Qs. Next steps: 1) Sofia sends pricing + security packet, 2) Michael sends streaming+retry sample code, Node and iOS, plus Optimize sample report, 3) Raj sends traffic profile and three canonical prompts, 4) Schedule POC kickoff next Tue.
20:54 Raj: Sounds good. We'll aim to send numbers by Monday.
21:00 Tina: Any final questions?
21:06 Priya: For the POC, what's the minimal committed spend?
21:10 Sofia: For hosted POC we typically use a consumption-based approach with a short-term estimated credit or a small reserved burst — we'll lay out options in the pricing email. For Dedicated you need a larger monthly commit.
21:28 Raj: Also want to confirm retention policy options — can we have 30-day logs then automatic purge?
21:34 Sofia: Yes, we support custom retention windows per-tenant; the security packet will include config steps.
21:46 Tina: Great.

22:00 [closing remarks]
22:05 Sofia: Thanks everyone, appreciate the time. We'll send the docs asap and propose times for next week.
22:12 Michael: Thanks.
22:16 Tina: Thank you.
22:20 [call ends]

Post-call notes (auto): transcription shows several mis-hearings — e.g., a few proper nouns were transcribed incorrectly (console trace ids). Action items assigned above.
